plot-data.t: Each dot is **one student**: **hours studied** on the x-axis and **exam score** on the y-axis. More hours tend to mean higher scores, so a line might describe the trend.

initialize.t: Our model is a line: **prediction = w × hours + b**. We start with **w = 0 and b = 0**, a flat line that predicts **0 for everyone**. This is only a starting guess.

predict.t: For each student the **prediction is the point where their hours meet the line**. Every prediction here is 0, far below the real scores.

error.t: The **error (residual)** is **actual score minus predicted score**: the vertical gap between a dot and the line. Big gaps mean the line fits that student badly.

loss.t: Squaring each error makes it positive and punishes big misses, and averaging gives one number: the **MSE**. **A big MSE means a poor fit**, and training tries to shrink it.

adjust.t: **Training changes w and b.** This new line is closer to the dots, so the errors and the **MSE are smaller**. The model learned by reducing its own error.

better-fit.t: With **w = 9 and b = 33** the line passes almost through every dot and the **MSE is only 0.4**. Learning a linear model means **adjusting w and b until the errors are as small as possible**.
